newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Eastern Zaire war refugess reach remote Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Eastern Zaire war refugess reach remote Kisangani.

text.p: Zaire war refugees began arriving in Kisangani on swollen feet on Thursday after fleeing the fighting far to the east, aid officials said.
"The first refugees have arrived in Kisangani. There are 50 or so, and they say there are hundreds behind on the road," said Claude Olenga, local administrator of church charity CARITAS.
"They are sick, their feet are swollen and all their belongings are gone," Olenga said. "We have no means of taking care of them -- no food, no medicine. It's a catastrophe."
Olenga told Reuters the 50 Zairean men and women said they had set out from Bukavu, one of three major east Zaire towns seized by Tutsi rebels in two weeks of fighting with the Zaire army.
The Zaireans said Rwandan Hutus, the majority of 1.2 million refugees dispersed from camps, had also heded for Kisangani but may have been blocked by local people.
Refugees arriving in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi reported people were dying of thirst in the harsh mountains of eastern Zaire.
Kisangani, 500 km (310 miles) from the eastern town of Goma that lies at the heart of the conflict, is the last major Zairean outpost before a vast stretch of hills and jungle.

It was used by France as a staging post in its 1994 military mission to save hundres of thousands of Hutus fleeing Rwanda after Hutu hardliners massacred up to a million Tutsis and their sympathisers. Diplomats say it is likely to play the same role if a French-inspired multinational rescue force is set up.

Hutus who feared revenge if they went home remained in camps in Zaire until dispersed by the current fighting, in which Zaire accuses Rwanda's Tutsi-led army of joining the Banyamulenge ethnic Tutsis.
It was not clear when the refugees left Bukavu. Fear and tension gripped the city long before Banyamulenge rebels stormed it soon after war erupted in the region on October 18.
Anti-Rwanda riots have spread to Kisangani and aid workers said the presence of Rwandan refugees in an area where food is acutely short was bound to fuel local resentment.
"The refugees hide themselves where they can because of the local people," Olenga said. "There is a serious food shortage here and it is fast approaching disaster."
Aid officials seeking news of refugees were trying to reach Lubutu -- halfway to Goma or Bukavu -- which they described as the tip of a creeping disaster.

"There is no fighting there but our reports say there are many people who fled from further east," said Jose des Chartes Menga of a local human rights group. "Many are wounded and there is a very real danger of diarrhoea or cholera epidemics."
Epidemics killed more than 1,000 refugees daily at one stage in Goma when the city was swarmed by Hutus in the 1994 exodus.
"We have very little contact with the region. All we know is that people have had to run away across the whole area," Menga added.
European Union aid ministers, stung by French criticism of "spineless inaction", met on Thursday to seek a joint response to the deepening human crisis.

France and Spain have proposed a multinational force of about 5,000 to secure corridors for food aid and passage of refugees to go home. The United States has offered logistics support, but no other Western nation has so far offered troops.

Kisangani was calm on Thursday after a day of violent protests by students who burned Rwandan-owned property and condemned their government's handling of the war. Tutsis effectively control the two Kivu provinces.
